source: video/script.md, Narration blocks. Text is verbatim; whitespace is normalized to single spaces.

act1.text: This is a plain terminal. No browser, no GPU window, just text.
FrankenTTY welds FFmpeg's modern video pipeline to the VT100 escape codes from the 1970s.
Every frame you see is characters and color codes, streamed with sound.

act2.text: One character cell holds two pixels: the half block's foreground is the top, its background the bottom.
We measured Apple Terminal taking in only about two and a half megabytes a second, and the real cost is color changes, not bytes.
So the encoder remembers what is already on screen, sends only changes, and reuses colors.
That cuts color codes by fifty-two to ninety-four percent, depending on the picture.

act3.text: M switches between half blocks, ASCII and Braille.
C cycles CRT palettes: amber, green phosphor, and a four-shade handheld look.
Seeking takes about a fifth of a second, and the sound comes back with the picture.
When the window grows past what the terminal can draw, a quality governor steps in: it merges close colors, then drops to 256 colors, then draws fewer cells.
Press q, and the terminal is exactly as you left it.

act4.text: FrankenTTY was built in Kiro by two agents.
Claude Opus 5.5 wrote the EARS specs, steering and task briefs, and reviewed every change.
Claude Sonnet 5.5 built each brief, often three at once in separate git worktrees.
Hooks ran the tests after every write and refused to end a turn until the suite was green.
Property-based tests caught two mistakes in the spec itself, and a clock bug.
A Kiro Power gives agents an MCP tool that renders a frame through a real terminal emulator.
CI builds for five platforms, and one command installs it.
